2.2.1.1 Riverbank Shrub Thicket
A definite riverbank shrub thicket community, dominated by alder (Alnus serrulata), is found in all gorges, forming a dense growth of varying width along the banks of all rivers and large creeks. It occurs both on rocky stream margins with little soil accumulation and on wider, sandy alluvial flats adjacent to the river. Willow (Salix nigra) is commonly associated with alder, but where streams are narrower and more shaded, rhododendron (Rhododendron maximum) is abundant. In broad, open rivers sweet gum (Liquidambar styraciflua) and sycamore (Platanus occidentalis) are found, and on narrower streams sweet birch (Betula lenta), hemlock (Tsuga canadensis), and tulip poplar (Liriodendron tulipifera) occur in a scattered distribution pattern. Shrub yellow-root (Xanthorrhiza simplicissima) is usually found along the water's edge. The most common understory herbaceous plants are sedges (Carex spp.), boneset (Eupatorium spp.), violet (Viola primulifolia), and bluet (Houstonia serpyllifolia).
2.2.1.2 Disturbed Floodplain Forest
The disturbed floodplain forest community occurs in alluvial flats between the riverbanks and gorge slopes that were once settled and are now abandoned. The soils are generally rocky and sandy, but these areas support substantial tree growth. Almost all these narrow flood plains lie below elevation 1,800 feet. Because they have a history of cultivation, the present vegetation is seral and somewhat heterogeneous. Below 1,400 feet, where the floodplains are broadest and sandiest, Virginia pine (Pinus virginiana) and white pine (P. strobus) are dominants. Associated deciduous trees are red maple (Acer rubrum), sweet gum, tulip poplar, hemlock, and sourwood (Oxydendrum arboreum). Many species of shrubs are found in the understory vegetation, such as mountain laurel (Kalmia latifolia), doghobble (Leucothoe axillaris var. editorum), blueberries (Vaccinium spp.) and blackberries (Rubus spp.). This community is best developed along the larger rivers (Toxaway, Horsepasture, and Chattooga Rivers). The climax community of these floodplain areas will probably be a mixed mesophytic, deciduous forest.
2.2.1.3 Mixed Mesophytic Forest
The coves and lower protected slopes of the escarpment gorges are occupied by a mixed mesophytic forest community, comprising two segregates: cove and slope. The cove segregate is composed of forests occupying the most mesophytic sites (cool, very humid environment) in the gorge area.
